title: The Funhe verses

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gatha, Guru Arjan's spoonful of honey. Your line was dense and short. Whose short sentence did you give the time of a long one? Day one thousand two hundred six.

Har haan. Two syllables, like a foot coming down at the turn of a dance step. Har haan. Right after the Gatha, on Ang thirteen hundred sixty-one, come Guru Arjan's Funhe, short verses that each turn on that same small refrain. Yesterday was about density, one line folded tight. Today is about rhythm, the same beat returning, verse after verse, the way a heart keeps time. And what that heart is keeping time for, it turns out, is someone it misses.
screen: `HAR HAAN.` → `RIGHT AFTER THE GATHA.` → `THE SAME BEAT RETURNING.`

segments.voice: The outline calls the Funhe short rhythmic verses of longing, and both halves matter. First, the rhythm. In each verse, the last line opens with har haan, a refrain that some explain as the Lord's name with a sung affirmation, something like yes, Lord. Because it comes back every time, the verses have a pulse you can feel even before you follow the meaning. Then, the longing. They open with an image, paraphrased: with pen in hand, the Inaccessible One writes on the forehead. From there the verses keep reaching toward the Beloved: the beauty of the Lord, the wish to meet, the sweetness of the holy company where the Name is sung. They're short enough that the longing never gets the chance to become a speech. It just keeps arriving, beat by beat. Why would longing want a rhythm? Missing someone can work like this. It doesn't come once and leave. It comes back on its own schedule, at the kettle, at the door, at the same hour each night. The Funhe give that returning a shape and a direction. Instead of being a wound that reopens, the return becomes a refrain, a place the heart keeps landing on purpose. Har haan. Har haan. Seen this way, a repeating line in kirtan isn't filler. It's the heart finding its footing, again.
screen: `A REFRAIN IN EVERY VERSE.` · `THE PEN ON THE FOREHEAD.` · `LONGING THAT KEEPS ARRIVING.` · `A RETURN WITH A DIRECTION.` · then, large: `RHYTHMIC LONGING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read three. If you can find the Funhe on Ang thirteen hundred sixty-one, read three of them, slowly, and let your voice drop a little on every har haan, like a step landing. If you can't, simply let the breath be the rhythm. In, and on the out-breath, the two syllables quietly: har haan. Don't force any feeling. Just let the beat come back, and back, and notice what it's reaching for. The bell holds the time.
The Funhe verses. Guru Arjan's short verses of longing, each one landing on the refrain har haan. Today's word.
Your line: rhythmic longing. Today, when a missing comes back, for a person, a place, for God, let it land like a refrain instead of a wound. Day one thousand two hundred six.

howItsDone: Guru Arjan's Funhe are read as part of the closing sections of the Guru Granth Sahib, and some are sung in kirtan, where the refrain har haan gives the singing its pulse.
